title: How Kenton and Herman made it work while Raeburn did not
summary: Schremp asks why leaders like Herman and Kenton succeeded; Handy says he has no right to judge Kenton.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Anyway, the three big bands were--

the only ones of any real significance.
My point in setting that up is
Woody was not a hell of a good player either,
but--

--Woody is a good editor. Also he had absolute trust in his players; his players have traditionally, for forty five years, hired all the new people. If you need a trumpet player, you ask your lead player to call a friend of his; that's the way that band does business.
Kenton, I think, was to the same extent. Kenton is not a great piano player, by any stretch, but an important writer of that era, but the point is they succeeded, both of them--
I didn't think that Kenton was a good writer.
He was a characteristic writer; he wrote the Kenton style and it stuck and it guided people. Is it fair to say it guided people? It established--
I really don't have the right to judge him, because I haven't heard all his music, and I haven't heard all his writing. I shouldn't have said that; I don't have a right to judge.
In any case, neither of these were technical giants, but they managed to make the band work by patching together what talent they had and what abilities they had.
Raeburn didn't-- Raeburn was in the same position, but didn't manage to make the band work in that same sense. Why? What did he not patch together, how could he have?
My reference to that is when you say that if they really recorded that material, which the band was known for, if you made that record, that you think it would have made a difference in his fate.
